content: After completing a four-week wheelchair skills training program, participants demonstrated significant improvements in both their wheelchair performance and safety. Below are the findings from various studies on wheelchair training programs: 1. Rice et al. (2017, USA): Pediatric manual wheelchair users (N=12) underwent transfer training with educational components, including video and feedback sessions. Compared to a group without educational training (N=7), the intervention group showed significant improvements in transfer performance. However, no changes were observed in self-perception variables three months post-training. 2. Rigot et al. (2021, USA): A web-based transfer training program for wheelchair users (N=34) improved transfer quality immediately after training and maintained improvements for at least one month. The control group (N=38) showed no such improvements. 3. Routhier et al. (2012, Canada): Adult manual wheelchair users (N=39) who received the French-Canadian version of the Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP) in addition to standard care showed immediate improvements in wheelchair skills, particularly at the community-skills level. Minimal decline was observed at follow-up, though sample size reduction limited statistical significance. 4. Sakakibara et al. (2013, Canada): Older adults inexperienced with manual wheelchairs (N=20) participated in two one-hour WSTP sessions. They reported increased confidence in wheelchair use, though no significant changes in participation were noted. 5. Van Der Scheer et al. (2016, Netherlands): Inactive manual wheelchair users with long-term spinal cord injuries (N=29) underwent 16 weeks of low-intensity wheelchair propulsion training. No substantial improvements in wheelchair skill performance were observed compared to usual care (N=14). 6. Worobey et al. (2018, USA): Both web-based and in-person transfer skills training for independent wheelchair users (N=87) resulted in improved transfer techniques compared to a waitlist control group (N=11). 7. Worobey et al. (2021, USA): Group wheelchair maintenance training for manual and power wheelchair users (N=188) improved their ability to perform maintenance tasks. These improvements were sustained for up to 12 months post-training. 8. Sawatzky et al. (2012, Canada): Children with spinal cord problems (N=6) who participated in a nine-hour WSTP over two days showed significant increases in wheelchair skills. They reported less pain and fatigue post-training, though no changes in participation were noted. 9. Kenyon et al. (2017, USA): Young children with severe impairments (N=3) demonstrated improved power mobility performance after a 12-week individualized training program using a shared control power mobility device. 10. Loomis & Boersma (1982, Canada): Adults with right cerebrovascular accidents (N=4) who received verbal mediation training during wheelchair drills showed improved performance, correct task sequencing, and fewer errors compared to those without verbal mediation. 11. Harrison et al. (2002, UK): Novice powered wheelchair users with neurological conditions (N=6) trained in virtual reality environments showed improved maneuverability and route-finding skills. 12. Adelola, Cox & Rahmana (2009, Ireland): Two children with cerebral palsy retained wheelchair driving skills acquired through virtual functional driving tasks over seven weeks. 13. Chang et al. (2020, China): Individuals with spinal cord injuries (N=130) who underwent two rehabilitation periods, including wheelchair skills training, showed significant improvements in basic life skills and their application in family and social life. 14. Bazant et al. (2015, Kenya and Philippines): Wheelchair-related training was associated with higher performance in activities of daily living in Kenya. In the Philippines, training was linked to fewer serious falls but not non-serious falls. 15. Stefenac et al. (2018, Croatia): Adult wheelchair users reported high satisfaction with wheelchair training, regardless of whether it was provided by medical or non-medical trainers. 16. Webster et al. (2001, USA): Patients with unilateral neglect (N=40) who underwent computer-assisted wheelchair training performed better on obstacle courses and had fewer incidents during hospitalization compared to controls. These studies collectively highlight the effectiveness of various wheelchair training programs in improving mobility, safety, confidence, and quality of life for users across different populations and settings.
